summary:
TerraGauge is an interactive decision map that helps Houston identify where changing ground conditions deserve added monitoring or immediate planning attention. We transformed ten years of NASA OPERA radar measurements and all 27 NASA-ISRO NISAR image pairs into a 13,299-cell map of Houston, then linked it to HoustonNet GPS, groundwater, soil compaction, and FEMA flood-zone records. We checked the satellite against 131 GPS stations, and the permanent ones agree to within about 1.7 mm a year. In fact, before we downloaded NISAR's 2026 data, we wrote down the sinking pattern it should show, and it did.

A planner can click any one-kilometer square to see the satellite evidence, confidence level, nearby monitoring coverage, relevant flood context, and recommended next steps. This matters in coastal cities like Houston: Hurricane Harvey caused $125 billion in damage, displaced more than 30,000 people, damaged or destroyed over 200,000 homes and businesses, and killed 89 people. NASA-supported research found that 85% of Harvey's flooded area had been sinking faster than 5 millimeters per year before the storm, and land that has sunk sits closer to the water that floods it.

TerraGauge makes that hidden land-motion evidence usable before the next storm exposes the gap. Its framework can be adapted for cities worldwide, where 1.81 billion people live in flood-prone areas and up to 1.6 billion people could face sinking land by 2040.
details:
Formal Research Paper: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bd9Ijv4hekemvfkvEvwemZAHVxt0nYgV/view?usp=sharing

Initially drafted using SI via the PaperOrchestra framework, this paper was subsequently reviewed and refined manually by all team members.

What does your project do, and how does it work?

TerraGauge turns satellite radar and ground measurements into clear, evidence-backed recommendations for Houston's planners, one square kilometer at a time.

It starts with ten years of NASA OPERA satellite measurements (2016–2026), collected by Europe's Sentinel-1 satellites, and all 27 NISAR image pairs taken over Houston so far. Our Python pipeline downloads the data directly from NASA, organizes measurements into one-kilometer squares, and tracks the source and processing history of every result.

Before measuring ground movement, TerraGauge filters out unreliable readings, including those over water, areas with weak radar signals, and patches the satellite cannot reliably connect to the rest of an image. It also checks whether NISAR has enough overlapping measurements to calculate a sinking rate. Since its current images form a simple chain without cross-checks, we don't claim a NISAR speed. Instead, we use NISAR for independent validation.

Using the ten-year radar record, TerraGauge calculates how quickly each square is sinking and compares it with surrounding areas. We validate these results against 131 GPS stations. Our primary comparison uses 64 permanent stations that were never used to calibrate the map. Satellite measurements agree with these stations to within approximately 1.7 mm per year, with a correlation of 0.68. We report results from the other 67 part-time stations separately.

We also conducted a blind NISAR test. Before downloading its 2026 data, we predicted that areas sinking fastest in the older radar record would also show the most movement in NISAR. Across 22 new image pairs and 1,287 squares, the prediction held: rank correlation was 0.60 across individual squares and 0.72 across 10-kilometer blocks. None of 10,000 random shuffles produced a comparable result.

Finally, TerraGauge combines radar measurements with GPS coverage, USGS groundwater wells, USGS soil compaction gauges, and FEMA flood zones. Each square receives one of six recommendations: Investigate first, Add monitoring here, Check the readings, Keep watching, No clear motion, or No measurement. It also identifies where additional GPS stations and low-cost sensors would fill the largest monitoring gaps. Every "Add monitoring here" square has a suggested monitoring site within 6 kilometers.

What benefits does your project provide?

Houston's ground-sinking data is scattered across different agencies, and raw satellite radar can be noisy and misleading. TerraGauge brings these sources together into one accessible map.

Each square includes supporting evidence, a confidence level, an explanation, the nearest GPS station, a five-year outlook, and a recommended next step. Rather than simply displaying where the ground is moving, TerraGauge helps identify where limited investigation and monitoring resources would have the greatest impact.

Just as importantly, it makes uncertainty visible. Weak or conflicting measurements are never presented as confirmed ground movement. We also tested our five-year outlook against nine forecasting methods using historical data. Our approach tied for the most accurate, while machine learning performed worst.

What is the intended impact of your project?

Houston shows why better ground monitoring matters. Parts of the region sank more than 10 feet during the 1900s as groundwater was pumped out. Today, TerraGauge identifies 1,715 sinking squares within FEMA high-risk flood zones that have no nearby GPS station.

NASA-supported research also found that 85% of the area flooded during Hurricane Harvey had been sinking faster than 5 mm per year. This is a correlation, not proof that sinking alone caused the flooding, but it demonstrates why ground movement belongs in flood planning.

TerraGauge aims to help cities detect changing ground conditions earlier, place limited monitoring equipment where it matters most, and make flood-resilience decisions using traceable evidence rather than black-box risk scores.

Planners can also identify areas where sinking has increased floodwater depth, where drought-related ground movement could threaten foundations and water mains, and where the ground sinks at very different speeds in neighboring areas, which can strain roads and pipes. Because TerraGauge uses open satellite data and local ground records, the same approach can be applied to other sinking cities monitored by NISAR.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software did you use?

Our data pipeline is written in Python 3.14 using NumPy, h5py, pyproj, rasterio, earthaccess, and scikit-learn. We also built 144 automated tests to validate the data and prevent the website from making claims that our measurements cannot support.

The website uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with MapLibre powering its interactive map and globe.

For hardware, we built a GroundTruth Node using a $74 Waveshare LC29H GPS receiver. We wanted to test whether an affordable GPS sensor could provide reliable enough measurements to expand monitoring in areas without existing stations. We processed its recordings against NOAA reference stations. Our first three sessions did not track enough satellites consistently to produce reliable results, so TerraGauge reports that limitation rather than presenting the readings as valid evidence.

What makes your project creative or innovative?

Most monitoring tools present a risk score or map. TerraGauge starts with raw satellite radar, tracks the origin of every measurement, validates it against independent ground data, and turns the results into specific actions planners can evaluate.

Its central innovation is connecting four questions that are usually handled separately:

  • Can we trust the satellite measurement?
  • Does it agree with measurements on the ground?
  • Where is uncertainty greatest?
  • What should a planner do next?

We also approached TerraGauge as a scientific investigation rather than just a software demonstration. We documented our methods and NISAR prediction before examining the results, validated satellite measurements against GPS stations never used for calibration, and selected our forecasting method by comparing nine approaches against historical data.

When evidence is incomplete or unreliable, the map makes that clear and identifies estimated squares instead of hiding coverage gaps.

What factors did your team consider during development?

We built TerraGauge around three priorities: accuracy, transparency, and usefulness in real-world decisions. Because satellite radar can be affected by weather, construction, and water, we paid particular attention to:

  • Signal quality and water interference.
  • Gaps in satellite and ground-station coverage.
  • Uncertainty in individual measurements.
  • The limitations of NISAR's first year of observations.
  • Areas where satellite and ground measurements disagree.

We were equally careful about what TerraGauge does not claim. It does not forecast floods, assume what caused ground movement, or treat a single radar image as proof of a hazard. Our outlook extends only five years because that is the period we could validate. The system distinguishes between "no data" and "no motion," identifies squares estimated from neighboring measurements, and reports hardware results that were not reliable enough to support a conclusion.

Finally, we kept the interface accessible to both technical users and the general public, including city planners and homeowners, and made sure it works on mobile devices. Every measurement and recommendation can be traced back to its source data and our publicly available code.
